key_terms.meaning: ∬_R f(x,y) dA = limit of Σ f(xᵢ,yᵢ) ΔAᵢ over a finer and finer partition of R
The tiny area piece; in Cartesian coordinates dA = dx dy
Two ordinary integrals done one after the other, such as ∫_a^b (∫_c^d f(x,y) dy) dx
For f continuous on R = [a,b] × [c,d], ∬_R f dA = ∫_a^b∫_c^d f dy dx = ∫_c^d∫_a^b f dx dy
Which variable is integrated first, written dy dx or dx dy
The set D in the plane over which the double integral is taken
D = {a ≤ x ≤ b, g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x)}: vertical strips, inner integral in y
D = {c ≤ y ≤ d, h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y)}: horizontal strips, inner integral in x
J = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) = det of the matrix of partials; then dA = |J| du dv
x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, with dA = r dr dθ and r ≥ 0
x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z, with dV = r dr dθ dz
x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, with dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ
∭_E f(x,y,z) dV, three nested ordinary integrals over a solid E
The plane region a solid casts on the xy-plane; it supplies the two outer limits
The tiny volume piece; in Cartesian coordinates dV = dz dy dx
Volume = ∬_D [top(x,y) − bottom(x,y)] dA over the shadow D

takeaways: A double integral is just a sum of small pieces f(x,y) ΔA in the limit, so every rule is bookkeeping on pieces.
Fubini turns one 2-D problem into two 1-D problems, and for a rectangle you may pick either order freely.
For a non-rectangular region, the limits are read off a sketch: outer limits are numbers, inner limits may depend on the outer variable.
Changing the order means redrawing the same region with strips running the other way; the value never changes, only the work does.
A change of coordinates multiplies the integrand by the absolute value of the Jacobian; forgetting |J| is the most common error.
Polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates exist to make circular, cylindrical and spherical regions simple, and their Jacobians are r, r and ρ² sin φ.
Triple integrals are set up outside-in: project the solid on a plane, then let the inner limits run from the lower surface to the upper surface.
Area is the double integral of 1 and volume is the triple integral of 1; both are special cases of the same idea.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are almost always 'set up correctly, then evaluate', so marks sit on the sketch, the correct limits and the Jacobian rather than on the final arithmetic.

bank.q: State Fubini's theorem for a rectangle and use it to evaluate ∬_R (x + 2y) dA over R = [0,1] × [0,2] in both orders.
outline: State the hypotheses: f continuous, R a closed rectangle.
Write both iterated forms.
Evaluate in dy dx order, showing the inner integral.
Repeat in dx dy order and confirm the same value.
Comment that equal answers are guaranteed by the theorem, not by luck.

bank.q: Define the double integral as a limit of Riemann sums and explain why dA = dx dy for a small rectangle.
outline: Partition the region into small rectangles of area ΔAᵢ.
Pick a sample point (xᵢ, yᵢ) in each piece and form Σ f(xᵢ,yᵢ) ΔAᵢ.
Take the limit as the mesh size tends to zero.
Show ΔAᵢ = Δx Δy for an axis-aligned rectangle.
State when the limit exists (f continuous on a bounded closed region).

bank.q: Explain the change-of-variables formula for double integrals and the role of the Jacobian.
outline: Write the map x = x(u,v), y = y(u,v) taking a region G to D.
Define J = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) as the 2×2 determinant.
State ∬_D f dA = ∬_G f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) |J| du dv.
Explain |J| as the local area-scaling factor of the map.
Mention that the map must be one-to-one inside G and C¹.

bank.q: Describe how limits for a triple integral over a solid are obtained by projection, and give the two possible orders.
outline: Project the solid E on the xy-plane to get D.
Outer two integrals run over D using the plane-region rules.
Inner integral in z runs from the lower surface z₁(x,y) to the upper surface z₂(x,y).
Also show the dz dy dx alternative where the first integration is in x.
Note that limits in the inner integral may depend on the two outer variables.

bank.q: Evaluate ∬_D (x + y) dA where D is the region between y = x² and y = x in the first quadrant.
outline: Find the intersection points of the two curves: (0,0) and (1,1).
Identify D as a Type I region: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, x² ≤ y ≤ x.
Integrate in y first: x(x − x²) + (x² − x⁴)/2.
Integrate the result from 0 to 1.
Final value 3/20.

bank.q: Change the order of integration in I = ∫₀¹ ∫_{x²}^{x} f(x,y) dy dx and write the new limits.
outline: Sketch: the region lies between y = x² and y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.
Fix y in [0,1]; the left boundary is x = y and the right boundary is x = √y.
New form: I = ∫₀¹ ∫_{y}^{√y} f(x,y) dx dy.
Check the corner points (0,0) and (1,1) lie on both descriptions.
State that the value of the integral is unchanged.

bank.q: By changing to polar coordinates, evaluate ∬_D e^{−(x²+y²)} dA over the quarter disc x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x² + y² ≤ a².
outline: Take x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, dA = r dr dθ.
Limits: 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.
Integrand becomes e^{−r²} and the extra factor r appears.
Substitute u = r², du = 2r dr and evaluate.
Answer (π/4)(1 − e^{−a²}).

bank.q: Using a double integral, find the volume of the solid above z = 0 and below z = 4, lying inside the cylinder x² + y² = 4.
outline: Shadow is the disc r ≤ 2; height at (r,θ) is 4.
Set up ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀² 4 r dr dθ.
Inner integral gives 8 per unit angle.
Result 16π cubic units with units stated.

bank.q: Evaluate ∭_E z dV where E is the solid cylinder r ≤ 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ 3, using cylindrical coordinates.
outline: Convert to r, θ, z with dV = r dr dθ dz.
Integrate in z first to get the factor 9/2.
Then ∫₀² r dr = 2 and ∫₀^{2π} dθ = 2π.
Result 18π.

bank.q: Find the mass of the semicircular lamina x² + y² ≤ a², y ≥ 0, whose density is ρ = k y.
outline: Write mass = ∬_D ρ dA over the semicircle.
Switch to polar: ρ = k r sin θ, dA = r dr dθ.
Limits: 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.
Integrate: (∫₀^a r² dr)(∫₀^π sin θ dθ) = (a³/3)(2).
Mass = 2ka³/3 with units of k stated.

bank.q: Evaluate ∭_E z dV where E is the tetrahedron with vertices (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1).
outline: The top face is the plane x + y + z = 1.
Inner integral gives (1 − x − y)²/2.
Middle integral gives (1 − x)³/6.
Final value 1/24.

bank.q: For D bounded by y = x², y = 2 − x and x = 0, set up ∬_D f dA in both orders and say which one you would choose for f = e^{y²}, with reasons.
outline: Sketch and find where y = x² meets y = 2 − x, i.e. x = 1, y = 1.
Type I: split the x-range at x = 1 because the upper boundary changes.
Type II: for 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, x runs from 0 to the curve x = √y for y ≤ 1 and x = 2 − y for y ≥ 1; or read x from the left boundary directly as a single formula if the sketch allows.
Argue that e^{y²} has no elementary antiderivative in y, so the x-first order is forced.
Show the resulting single integral in y that can be calculated.

bank.q: Derive the volume element in spherical coordinates from the Jacobian and use it to prove that the volume of a sphere of radius a is 4πa³/3.
outline: Write x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ.
Compute the 3×3 Jacobian determinant and simplify to ρ² sin φ.
State dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ and explain the geometric meaning of each factor.
Set limits 0 ≤ ρ ≤ a, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
Integrate to get (a³/3)(2)(2π) = 4πa³/3.

bank.q: Compare Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical set-ups for the volume of the solid inside the sphere x² + y² + z² = 4a² and inside the cylinder x² + y² = a², and evaluate the easiest one.
outline: Note the solid is symmetric about z = 0, so double the part with z ≥ 0.
Cylindrical: 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ z ≤ √(4a² − r²).
Evaluate 2∫₀^{2π}∫₀^a √(4a² − r²) r dr dθ by substituting u = 4a² − r².
Result (4πa³/3)(8 − 3√3).
Explain why spherical limits would need a split in φ where the sphere meets the cylinder, making it harder.

glossary.def: The limit of a sum of f values times small areas over a plane region.
Two single integrals nested, evaluated from the inside out.
A continuous function on a rectangle can be integrated in either order with the same result.
The infinitesimal element of area in a double integral.
The infinitesimal element of volume in a triple integral.
The plane region or solid over which a multiple integral is taken.
A region described by vertical strips, with x limits constant.
A region described by horizontal strips, with y limits constant.
The sequence in which the nested single integrals are performed.
The determinant of the matrix of first partial derivatives of a coordinate map.
Rewriting an integral in new coordinates, multiplying by the absolute Jacobian.
Plane coordinates (r, θ) with x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
Polar coordinates in the xy-plane plus the usual z height.
Coordinates (ρ, θ, φ) with ρ the distance from the origin and φ the angle from the z-axis.
The shadow a solid casts on a coordinate plane, used to fix outer limits.
A thin flat plate treated as a plane region with a density function.
Mass per unit area for a lamina, or per unit volume for a solid.
The point where the whole mass may be treated as concentrated; found with first moments.
The integral of density times squared distance from an axis.
An integral over an unbounded region or with an unbounded integrand, defined by a limit.
A finite sum of function values times cell sizes that approaches the integral.
The largest cell dimension in a partition; the double integral is the limit as it goes to zero.
